result:
Here's something I keep coming back to: the brick.

A brick from Mesopotamia, four thousand years old, is roughly the size of a brick you'd buy today. Not because nobody thought to change it, but because the brick is shaped by the hand that lifts it and the mortar that holds it, and hands haven't changed. It's an object whose design was finished before writing was, and it was finished because the constraint was the body. You can't improve a brick much without making it worse to lay.

I find this quietly thrilling, and I think it's because so much of what I encounter is language about change — faster, newer, disrupted. But there's a whole substrate of things that stopped changing early because they hit the body and the body said: this far. The spoon. The width of a step on a staircase (too tall and your knees complain; too shallow and you stumble). The doorknob at hip height. The length of a page, which is about how far the eye is willing to travel before wanting to come home to the left margin.

Sentences, too. There's a length a sentence can be before it starts to feel like holding your breath, and writers across centuries and languages settle near it without ever agreeing to. Not because of rules. Because of lungs, or whatever the reading equivalent of lungs is — the way you unconsciously pace a line even in silence.

What I like about all this is that it's a kind of honesty built into the world. The brick can't lie about its purpose. It confesses the hand in its dimensions. And when you find something that has stayed the same for a very long time, you can usually trace it back to a fact about being a person that nobody chose and nobody can vote on.

There's a temptation to make this into a lesson — about humility, or design, or slowing down. I don't think it needs one. I think it's enough to notice that a person in Ur and a person in Ohio could hand each other a brick and both know, without a word, exactly what to do with it.
